speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce one or two questions regarding Microsystems International which I have raised on previous occasions. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have the answer to that additional question this morning but I may answer the previous questions which were posed. The hon. member referred to lay-offs at that time by Microsystems. My information is that there have been no lay-offs at Microsystems since December, 1971, nor are there liable to be as sales are increasing at this time.
He questioned me also on the monitoring of research and development funds provided by my department. This is indeed being done very closely, and careful consideration is given to all expenditures of government funds to ensure optimum returns to Canada. I might add that last year 78 per cent of sales of Microsystems were to Northern Electric, but this percentage is decreasing as overseas sales in particular expand. My friend may have seen the recent agreement between Microsystems and some Japanese companies. Losses are also decreasing and cannot be attributed to their sales to Northern Electric. These losses are start-up costs.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED EROSION OF PARLIAMENT'S CONTROL OVER GOVERNMENT SPENDING AS A RESULT OF EVASION OF CONSTITUTIONAL SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
This House, noting the continuing erosion of Parliament's control over government spending of public moneys due to government evasion of constitutional and legal safeguards as noted in the 1970-71 report of the Auditor General, and due to imperfect procedural structure, reaffirms the fundamental principle of the Canadian constitution that parliament must control expenditures of public moneys.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think it is a terrible indictment of this government that in this year A.D. 1972 the parliamentary opposition feels compelled to move, in terms of this kind, a motion such as the one Your Honour has just read. It is not the first time this has happened. Two years ago, on April 21, 1970, my leader moved a motion in not quite the same terms but along the same general lines. This motion included the following statement:
That this House condemns the government for criticizing the Auditor General of Canada for carrying out his duties according to law; and reasserts its support of the principle of unfettered parliamentary scrutiny of government expenditures-
And so on. As I say, that was two years ago. Since that time a lot of water has gone under the bridge. There have been two more annual reports issued by the Auditor General and Tabled in this House. I think it is a shocking thing that at this time we should be compelled to move such a motion.
Two years ago, on April 21, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), in replying on behalf of the government-as I assume he will again today-made this statement as reported at page 6119 of Hansard. After referring to the motion, he said:

May 26, 1972
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys
This statement puts forward principles which are unexceptionable.
Obviously it would appear that the government and the hon. gentleman accepted those principles. I thought at the time, going back to a Biblical quotation from, I think, Luke, that there is more joy in heaven over one Liberal sinner who has repented-and I see another leaving the House at this time-than seventy and two just Conservatives who needed no repentance.
When we read the Auditor General's report that has so recently been placed in our hands, it is obvious that there was no real belief on the part of the President of the Treasury Board in what he said at that time. As a matter of fact, when we read his speech of April 21, 1970, as well as a similar speech that he made on another occasion, I think I was deluded in accepting in good faith his statement that this principle was one which was unexceptionable. I say that because, as reported at page 6121, the President of the Treasury Board went on to say this:
We will be proposing that the government ought to be obliged to report to Parliament, to the Public Accounts Committee, on the totality of the Auditor General's report, on all the criticisms he has made of the government and the public service.
Raising its ugly head at that time was the intention of the government, which has now been confirmed, that it should have the opportunity to rebut in advance of presentation to this House the statements made by the Auditor General, an official of parliament who reports to this House. The government, obviously angered, worried and concerned, as it should properly be, about these very reasonable criticisms that had been made over and over again, was planning to try to reduce the effect of those criticisms by making a rebuttal in advance, instead of following the proper practice of having its representative appear before the public accounts committee.
On another occasion, namely on March 7, 1972, we found it necessary to bring forward another motion in my name, not in the same terms as this, of course, but dealing with the same general issue. At that time the President of the Treasury Board told us exactly what the government thought of the attempts made by this party and the House to look into this matter. As reported at page 606 of Hansard for that date the President of the Treasury Board made this statement:
After the next election we undoubtedly will have another look at this problem of the allocation of our most valuable commodity, time, and will have noted the experiences of the present parliament.
That is a clear and present threat by the President of the Treasury Board that if after the next election this country is unfortunate enough to have another Liberal government, which would include the hon. gentleman and, I assume, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as members, then there will be an attempt to restrict opportunities for parliament to examine the very important issues that should be examined. I say that is a clear threat by the hon. gentleman, and I hope that the members of his own party, as well as the public, will take note of it. This, Mr. Speaker, is their reply to debates of this sort that we have launched in a statesmanlike way to try to secure some reasonable and rational discussion of this very serious problem.

I could go back to the British North America Act and to the Financial Administration Act to outline these principles which have been established over the generations. It is the right of the representatives of the people, and not the right of the Treasury Board or the government, to scrutinize and examine the expenditures of government to ensure that the government proceeds according to the accepted principles and practices of parliamentary dominance in so far as the expenditure of public money is concerned. This government has forgotten, if it ever knew, that these principles exist.
What was the reaction of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) yesterday? I raised this matter and other hon. members pursued it in the House during the question period as well as outside. What did the Prime Minister suggest as a remedy? The right hon. gentleman was going to arrange for the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) to refer the report to the Public Accounts Committee. In heaven's name, what is the situation now of the Public Accounts Committee? Because of slovenliness, incompetence, indecision, inability or a lack of desire on the part of the government to get the Auditor General's report of previous years into the hands of the Public Accounts committee in the proper time, the Public Accounts Committee is now months behind in its study of the 1970 report. That report has only been very scantily digested. There has not been adequate opportunity to do very much about that report. The Public Accounts Committee is still charged with and engaged in looking into this report.
I know the government will say the Auditor General had some responsibility because his report did not come into the hands of the government in time. I deny that allegation and refute it in advance, because I can see by the look in the eyes of the President of the Privy Council that this is what he is going to say. If the Auditor General did not get his report into the hands of the government in the proper time on occasions, he has made it abundantly clear by statements in the Public Accounts Committee and elsewhere that it was because this government, whether deliberately or by inadvertence, has failed to provide him with the staff and equipment he needs to do his job. That is where the fault lies, right at the door of the government, and it cannot hide behind any such statement. In any event, it will probably be weeks or months, knowing the way this government is operating, before the Public Accounts Committee is able to complete its deliberations and make its reports in respect of the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1971.
What consummate duplicity on the part of gentlemen opposite to suggest that the answer to our legitimate complaints and the answer to the anxiety, frustration and anger of the people of Canada about this continuing example of unparallelled government extravagance, waste and stupidity in the expenditure of our money is this reference of the Auditor General's Report for 1971 to the Public Accounts Committee. This Chamber is the place in which people should be looking at the case made by the Auditor General, not in respect of the items, but in respect of his statement that there is a continuing erosion by the government of the right of this Parliament to
May 26, 1972

control funds which are expended by the government of Canada.
Let me buttress that statement by reference to the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1971. The Auditor General writes in paragraph 50, at page 22:
Reference was made in paragraph 47 of our 1970 report to the inclusion in the 1969-70 Estimates of amounts which were not required to meet expenditure coming in course of payment during that year.
I pause there to emphasize the fact that the Auditor General is saying, in his current report, that this is not the first time he has brought to the attention of this House and the people of Canada a very serious allegation in respect of the government. In the 1970 report, there was paragraph 47, which I will not bother to read as it is along the same lines.
The Auditor General goes on to say in paragraph 50 of his 1971 report:
Nevertheless they were recorded as expenditure of the year under the authority of special wording in the several vote texts in the Appropriation Acts. These amounts, totalling $172,685,000, formed part of certain balances totalling $296,663,000 at March 31, 1970 which were available without further reference to Parliament to meet obligations coming in course of payment subsequent to that date. We pointed out that one of the most important controls exercised by Parliament over public expenditure was provided by section 20 of the Financial Administration Act which directs that:
"All estimates of expenditures submitted to Parliament shall be for the services coming in course of payment during the fiscal year."
In plain defiance of that Act of Parliament, the financial bible under which this government or any government of Canada should be operating, this government has arrogated the right to spend millions of dollars without obtaining the consent of this Parliament. The same situation prevailed in respect of the previous year.
The Auditor General has placed side by side at page 24, in the continuation of his description in paragraph 50, the sums of money which were available to this government to spend without proper appropriation or approval by this Parliament; one year it was $291 millions and in another year $296 million.
The Auditor General ends up with this statement:
We reiterate our view that one of the most important controls exercised by Parliament over public expenditure is its requirement that all estimates of expenditure submitted to it shall be for the services coming in course of payment during the fiscal year. This control is seriously weakened when funds are credited to special accounts to be available for spending in future years.
Then, the Auditor General goes on in the next paragraph to deal with the government contingencies program. We have had a lot of debate in the committee about this enormous special fund which, from year to year, aggregates well over $100 million. In the supplementary estimates, and I refer to supplementary estimates (B) for the year 1971-72, under the heading of "Treasury Board", there is an item, Vote 5b, government contingencies. The government, through the medium of this particular supplementary estimate, completely altered the purposes for which the vote of $75 million had been made available as part of the contingencies fund. I know it can be said that this Parliament did approve this item. This Parliament was bulldozed into approving it.
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys
What happens and how is this approval obtained? We all know that when there are supplementary estimates they are submitted to the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee which does not have a great deal of time to consider them. There are usually several hundreds of millions of dollars, involving many departments, and there is pressure on the committee to approve these estimates in order that they may qualify for passage under our Standing Orders. Here is an important deletion involving $75 million, and the committee has an extremely limited amount of time to debate it. There was no opportunity for the House to debate it. These are just illustrations. If I had time I could go through the Auditor General's report from back to front and give even more abundant examples than I have.
There is one more aspect of the government's failure to comply with the proper practices and rules of parliamentary control; that is, the method of legislating through the estimates for large sums of money to be paid out according to the whim of the government. I will give one or two examples. In Supplementary Estimates (A) for 1971-72, at page 44, there is a very large appropriation of some $160 million. This is the device used by the government for the granting of loans to provinces, provincial agencies and municipalities under the Municipal Development and Loan Act for the purpose of assisting in the creation of employment in accordance with terms and conditions set out in agreements entered into between the Minister of Finance and the provinces.
What that means is that the Minister of Finance enters into agreements with the provinces, which are never approved by this House, and which do not constitute any realistic attempt to cope with unemployment, which everybody agrees should be done. I feel very strongly that there should be some greater measure of consultation with Parliament when an amount of $160 million is expended merely by placing an item in the estimates rather than giving Parliament the opportunity it would have had to debate that item had it been contained in a bill. Hon. members know that there is a debate on second reading of a bill, after which it is referred to a committee. There is an opportunity to call witnesses, make proposals and move amendments. The bill then returns to the House for the report and third reading stages. Every stage is calculated to permit a diligent and effective opposition to deal with proposals of this kind and suggest alternative or additional means of coping with a problem.
Again, this procedure is not followed. The government all too often does this through the medium of an item in the estimates, in this case $160 million, and we have a further erosion of that Parliamentary control which is essential if Parliament is to retain any significance at all in the democratic process. I know that emergencies arise, at which time governments must act swiftly and it is not always possible to come to Parliament to secure the requisite consent. However, there is a very heavy burden on any government when it takes some $17 billion or $18 billion of the taxpayer's money out of their pockets every fiscal year without going to Parliament. I say these are the means an alert, intelligent and vigilant government would use to bring in legislation in ample time to permit the type of debate we should have. I deplore that practice which

May 26, 1972
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys
prevents this being done. I have referred to the means by which the government is gradually getting away from the type of control we ought to maintain.
There are other illustrations of this type of legislation by estimate which are indicative of an exceedingly bad practice. This is done by all governments. I believe it is about time we called attention to the fact that the members of this House and the country will no longer countenance such a practice. In addition to the Auditor General, the Public Accounts Committee has looked into this practice. As long ago as the year 1966-67, in the 13th report of the Public Accounts Committee, the committee looked at the general question of parliamentary control, filed a caveat and called the attention of the House and inferentially of the country to the fact that there was a weakening of parliamentary control. This was in another context, but it was done after very careful consideration. I took the time to read the minutes of proceedings and evidence which preceded the recommendation of the Public Accounts Committee. This recommendation was neglected. Nothing was done about it. This recommendation is one of 38 others which at the present time are lying untended. No action has been taken on them. The government either has neglected or rejected them, or is simply incapable of action on them.
The blue ribbon committee of this House charged with the responsibility of examining the public accounts through the medium of the Auditor General's report is a committee which, up until recent years, at any rate, has had a very enviable reputation for non-partisan objective examination in carrying out its duties. Here we have 38 recommendations going back to the fourth report in 1963. For nine years the recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee have been piling up, and we now find at this time that 38 of them have been neglected or rejected. This is the stage at which the Prime Minister was willing to leave the 1971 Auditor General's report. I had the honour of serving as chairman of the Public Accounts Committee for several years. I thoroughly enjoyed it. I believe it was a very responsible committee. I must say, however, that in recent years there has been some falling off of the spirit of non-partisanship which did exist and which always should be present in the committee.
The other day, while re-reading the story of Becket and King Henry II, I wondered whether the Prime Minister, having just finished reading a copy of the Auditor General's report of two years ago, said to those around him, "Is there no one who will rid me of this man?" I think those words are similar to the words of King Henry when he wanted to get rid of the Archbishop of Canterbury. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), the then President of the Privy Council, and the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) who was then I believe the government House leader, were quite eager to volunteer to make comments about the Auditor General which were not in keeping with their high responsibilities as ministers of the Crown. They were prepared to appear before the Public Accounts Committee and make remarks before that committee which would have had the effect of seriously crippling the function of the Auditor General of making a very impartial study.

There is no question in my mind, as a result of my appearances at the committee and reading the transcript of the proceedings, that there has been a greater disposition on the part of government members on that committee to attempt to hide some of the misdeeds of this government. I hope this is only temporary and will change. However, there are very few lines of defence left to the harassed taxpayer. By reason of certain changes in the rules, with respect to which some of my colleagues will later be dealing, the opportunities in this House are becoming increasingly restricted for dealing in the way in which we should be dealing with the right of this parliament to continue to exercise control over the public purse. The Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee, with which he works in the closest liaison, are probably the front line of defence the taxpayer has. I would hope- and I say this quite sincerely-that what I seem to have detected as a form of more aggressive partisan conduct on the part of government members of the committee will be changed and that they will return to the objective and impartial study which is essential if the committee is to do its job.

I am sorry the hon. member is so sensitive, but since he is attending the committee continuously he might be better qualified that I am to name the hon. members on his own side who are not non-partisan. However, I believe in the value and efficacy of this committee; there is no doubt about it. Obviously, we are getting so close to an election now that it is very unlikely this committee will be able to complete its deliberations, even on the 1970 report. I hope that after the next election when this parliament reconvenes, regardless of which party forms the government, the new public accounts committee will put behind it the bickering and partisanship which have crept into it which I say, in spite of what the hon. member has to say, does exist and can be easily detected.
One more point raised by the Auditor General is the question of his staff. This has been a continuing irritant. It has been referred to for over ten years. There has been an obvious need to secure a more effective method by which the Auditor General will be able to select his staff. I will not get into the details of it. I hope that either this government or the government that succeeds it will put together a new bill. I think we have to take the Auditor General out of the Financial Administration Act. When that new bill is put together, many of the proposals which have been
May 26, 1972

advocated by the Auditor General and his staff and which in many cases have been approved by the committee, should be contained in it. I should like to make reference only to page 4 of the report for this year where I find the following statement, but because my time is running short I will read only the last sentence of the paragraph. The Auditor General is referring there to the action of the Treasury Board in downgrading 28 senior members of his staff:
In my opinion, this action by the Treasury Board Secretariat is unfair and discriminates against the Auditor General. It should be corrected forthwith. If it is allowed to stand it will mean that his office is prevented from employing auditors in the highest classification in the public service of Canada. It will also mean that in order to reach the highest classification in their profession, his most experienced auditors must leave the office of the Auditor General.
I sincerely hope that when the new legislation is introduced this will be one of the problems which, along with others, will be solved.
I see that my time is close to being up. I want to close on this note. I know that when people occupy treasury benches, particularly those who have served previously in the establishment, in the civil service, they have a disposition to assume that they are the sole arbitrators of the way money is spent. I concede to them the essential right to initiate programs of expenditures

that is their duty and responsibility as the executive. But they move from that position to gradually assuming that they are lords of all they survey, that parliament exists only to be a rubber stamp for their wishes and views. They assume that members of parliament have no right to challenge their decisions regarding the expenditures of the public funds. The sole right of making decisions does not rest on the Prime Minister, on the President of the Treasury Board, on me, on the leader of my party or on any single member of this parliament; it rests with all the people of Canada. But the elected representatives sitting in the House are the people who, more nearly and more truly, are able to judge what the people of Canada wish in their infinite strength and wisdom, and I suggest-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED EROSION OF PARLIAMENT'S CONTROL OVER GOVERNMENT SPENDING AS A RESULT OF EVASION OF CONSTITUTIONAL SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this discussion of the motion which the official opposition has put before the House, I would first like to sketch the background against which it seems to me the Auditor General's report and the spendings of the vast and varied departments and agencies of government, should be reviewed.
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys
It is quite clear that the public sector spending at all levels of government constitutes the biggest big business in the country. In this place we are the trustees of the spending of the public's $15 billion or $16 billion of tax money a year. The government is into a variety of enterprises and services. The public is involved, through its agency the Post Office, in the delivery of millions of letters every day, the ownership and operation of thousands of motor vehicles in the service of various departments. The public is concerned and involved in the rubber business, the mining business, the housing, highway and even the movie business.
One item which we approved at this level some years ago had to do with the cost of construction of the National Arts Centre. By my calculation every Canadian man, woman and child was involved in the expenditure of approximately $2.20 to put the National Arts Centre here in our capital. In this way my own riding of Surrey-White Rock contributed through taxation something in the order of a quarter of a million dollars for the building of the National Arts Centre.
As one of our party's representatives on the Public Accounts Committee I feel at every session of that committee that I am plugged in, so to speak, to everybody's pocketbook and on the other hand to everybody's wellbeing. The same principles apply at the level of the Public Accounts Committee as they do at the level of the directors of a business or an association, the trustees of a church, or the officers of a trade union. We are all concerned with what we take in and what we put out. In our case, at this level of financial control or investigation, we should note that a great part of the billions we oversee are fixed charges. Defence and interest payments seem to be firmly in that category. Together, they make up about one fourth of our entire federal spending. In my view our spending in both these areas could be materially reduced by no more revolutionary a means than that employed by any sensible economically minded married couple. However, in line with all this, Mr. Speaker, and checking into the intricate and sometimes duplicative efforts and facilities of the federal government and it agencies, we have the Auditor General and his staff delving into and exposing the hundreds of items of governmental goofs and wastes.
The Public Accounts Committee recently compiled an historical record, extending from 1930 to 1970, of all the recommendations of the various public accounts committees over that 40 year period. It is a book of some size, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure it will make very interesting, if painful, reading. It is a history of waste exposed, and in too many instances left to continue. As a former newspaperman I can very well appreciate such juicy items as the ones featured in the press yesterday under the heading "Henderson's Horrors"-items about the mothballed hydrofoil that cost Canadians $8 per family, about the Prime Minister's flights, about the puppets that didn't puppet. But while we cry out at this waste of public money-money that could have been put to good use such as increasing the well-being of our older or younger people, or such as reducing the taxation of our middle

May 26, 1972
Alleged. Loss of Control of Public Moneys aged people-while we cry out at this cataloguing of bungling and waste, that is not enough.
There are two other areas in regard to the revelations in the Auditor General's report which must be objected to in the highest degree. The first is the revelation which the report makes of the government's tendency, (a) to put special wording into the vote texts of appropriation acts, and (b) to record certain items as expenditures duly approved by parliament which were in fact funds retained for spending in subsequent years and which should have gone back to parliament for re-approval. Millions of dollars have been secured by the government in this way in the 1970-71 period. This strikes at parliament's right to represent the public in the outlay of the public's money. This must be stopped. We recommend that where any change occurs in the normal course of presentation of estimates, in the wording or standards which previously prevailed, a note or other indication calling attention to the variation be included in that particular item. That would be a guide to parliament rather than, as has sometimes been the case, a blind to parliament.
Again, Mr. Speaker, dealing with the millions of dollars that the government gets by contingency votes for supplementing the appropriations of the various departments, back in 1966 the Public Accounts Committee urged that any additional amounts required by each department must be made the subject of a supplementary estimate, prepared by the department concerned for submission to parliament. If that procedure were carried out, it would put an end to the evasion of parliamentary control of public funds by the building up of reserves through contingency votes.
A second serious thing about the report of the Auditor General is the effect of the disclosures of the inefficiency, sloth and wastefulness which are present in some departments of government. The effect of this will be to the discredit and disdain of our parliamentary system. I wonder what the farmer, the logger, the fisherman, the plant or office worker, or the old age pensioner must think of parliament after this catalogue of waste. I wonder what the country must think of parliament, never mind what it thinks about the government, after reading the Auditor General's detailed, yet limited because of staff problems, report. It seems to me that the disclosures by the Auditor General strike at the root of the public's faith in their elected representatives. I believe that this House, the Public Accounts Committee, and particularly the government should put an end to the kind of thing which is exposed by the Auditor General. If we do not do so we will in effect be guilty of undermining the parliamentary system.
In the view of the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, all hon. members of this House should be united in their concern over the waste that the Auditor General exposes, and in many cases exposes every year without result. We should see to it that more power is given to the Auditor General, and that his staff is not handicapped, but indeed enlarged and upgraded, to find out and eliminate the inefficiency and waste which are tabulated in his report. We in the New Democratic Party are not content to exclaim over the scores of detailed items of non-produc-

tive expenditures as tabulated by the Auditor General. We are all for attacking them, and we do so in and out of committee, but that is not enough. I think we need to do two more things if the war on waste at the Ottawa level is to be won.
We need to follow up and follow through on the Auditor General's recommendations against leaks in public funds. His report states that of the 41 recommendations which had not been implemented or otherwise dealt with at March 31, 1970, 31 still remain. Seven additional recommendations are capable of specific implementation, but have not yet been implemented even though they were made by the Public Accounts Committee. The House should concern itself more than has been the case in pressing the government to expedite the implementation of the anti-waste recommendations of the Auditor General and of the Public Accounts Committee. We need to follow through to see that the leaks are blocked. But that too, important as it is, is not enough.
In my opinion we should press for a deep, broad and far-going survey, or inquiry or investigation of the system of the government's ways of doing business. It is not sufficient for us to examine the fruits of the system, not enough to take up individual results of a basic and continuing fault. We must get to the root as well as to the fruit of federal incompetence. I believe that the Auditor General himself made a rather similar proposal. In the Public Accounts Committee we read from year to year his reports of individual instances of bungling, but from year to year the same stream of dereliction continues to flow. I urge, in addition to the motion before us, that parliament either through the Public Accounts Committee, or perhaps through a select committee, should probe into the depths of the iceberg, the tip alone of which shows itself in the Auditor General's report. We should probe into this faulty system. Let us examine and correct the system, and not just complain about what it produces.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, we of the NDP support the motion moved by the Official Opposition. We press for more power and freedom of action for the Auditor General, and we intend to make detailed representations on that point at the committee level. We seek practical safeguards to stop the government's tendency to evade parliament's scrutiny and understanding of its accounts. We ask for a determination by all hon. members to follow through and see to it that the anti-waste recommendations are implemented. Finally, we call for an in depth inquiry into the system that produces the on-going waste and bungling in the expenditure of public funds.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) moved today is most important because it deals with the report the Auditor General of Canada presents every year. Every time this report comes out, we note that he points out innumerable costly errors for which civil servants are responsible
Every year the Auditor General presents a report which, to my mind, is revolting. If the Canadian public were to read it, I believe a revolt would break out in
May 26, 1972

Canada. In fact, this report points out the costly errors made by people who think they are competent and honest.
I feel the errors are deliberate in most cases. A person can make an error once, but when the error is repeated, one can wonder about the honesty of some civil servants.
Following the submission of those reports, we unfortunately note that there is a certain rivalry between the Auditor General and the government. Indeed, it became obvious a few months ago when the government blamed the Auditor General for failing to submit his report in time.
The Auditor General stated why it was late, as he had already done on many occasions at the end of several financial years.
At the beginning of the report which has just been given to us, the Auditor General mentions once again the difficulties he experiences when auditing public accounts. I will quote in that connection the last two paragraphs of section 8 on page 4 of the report which in my opinion are liable to throw some light on the situation. They are as follows:
In my opinion, this action by the Treasury Board Secretariat is unfair and discriminates against the Auditor General. It should be corrected forthwith. If it is allowed to stand it will mean that his Office is prevented from employing auditors in the highest classification in the Public Service of Canada. It will also mean that in order to reach the highest classification in their profession, his most experienced auditors must leave the Office of the Auditor General.
This is the position as it stands. The Auditor General is denied the right to hire the staff he needs and to determine their salaries at his discretion. This makes it very difficult for him to find the qualified staff he requires and even prevents him from retaining the one he presently has. If these employees want a pay increase or an improvement in their working conditions or of their situation, to which every federal civil servant is entitled as would be any other employee of the private sector or of an other level of government, they have no choice but to leave the Auditor General's Office and seek another job in private concerns or in government departments.
I proceed with my quotation from paragraph 8 of the report:
This action points up more clearly than anything else that if the Auditor General of Canada is to be truly independent he must be free to recruit the staff he needs and to determine their salary levels within the framework of the Public Service of Canada.
This is the situation, Mr. Speaker. Working conditions in the Auditor General's office are really difficult. Apparently it needs at least 28 or 30 officials to attain the necessary strength to perform worthwhile duties expected to be done within reasonable time.
Mr. Speaker, yet the Auditor General's office manages fairly well to audit all the departments' books. Maybe it does not work under the best of conditions but it succeeds just the same in making audits and in pointing out operating and management faults within these departments. Each year the Auditor General's report is studied by a committee especially set up for this purpose and whose chairman is chosen among the official opposition members so as to make it as unprejudiced as possible, it seems. In turn the Public Accounts Committee brings in each
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys year several reports and makes recommendations to the government. But the government is reluctant to accept and implement these recommendations.
The report of the Auditor General for this year mentions at least 38 recommendations of the Committee on Public Accounts that still lie idle and have not been implemented. And one wonders whether the government or some of its departments have at least examined them.
Mr. Speaker, in view of this situation, we have no other alternative than to ask once more the Committee on Public Accounts to scrutinize the report of the Auditor General of Canada, to make once more to the government recommendations that it will deem fair and necessary. Let us hope that the next government whatever it may be will take steps to implement these recommendations and to grant the Auditor General of Canada and his staff all the freedom required to perform their duties adequately, for we hold the view that the office of the Auditor General of Canada is in a certain way the keeper of the nation's business. He has a duty to reveal publicly mistakes that have been made, to make suggestions and to trust that the government will correct the situation.
If you consider all the amounts that have been spent unnecessarily by the various government departments, you realize that millions of dollars have been spent uselessly. Here is one more reason to be concerned over this situation which has been recurring year after year without the government doing anything about it.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I hope the government will give more special consideration to the recommendations made in this report, as well as to those of the public accounts committee.
Unless steps are taken, the Canadian public will increasingly lose confidence in this nation's administration, and this could have serious consequences.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I again urge the government to accept the Auditor General's main recommendation that he be given all possible freedom in the hiring of his staff, and at the same time, that he be allowed to keep the qualified staff which is now serving him , in the interests of highest efficiency.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time of the adjournment for lunch, I was mentioning some of the actions proposed to Parliament and some of the actions directly taken by the government to improve substantially the capacity of Parliament, particularly the House of Commons, to scrutinize in an effective way the programs and activities of the government. I indicated that I would make a rather more detailed reference to this in the current period. The first reference I would like to make is to the new system of supply which, as I indicated earlier, seems to have been imperfectly understood by the hon. member for Peace River in his speech proposing this motion. May I refer the House to a very excellent pamphlet entitled "How Your Tax Dollar is Spent, 1972-73". The first part of this pamphlet is entitled "Parliament is Supreme" and I suggest this conveys an understanding and a belief of the government.
In indicating the kind of new supply arrangements that have been adopted by the House, the pamphlet has this to say:
From Confederation in 1867 through to 1968, the Canadian House of Commons considered these estimates in what was called the Committee of Supply. This Committee was composed of all
May 26, 1972

members of the House and carried out its work in the Commons Chamber. Because only Members of Parliament are allowed to speak in the chamber, no outside witnesses or public servants could be heard or questioned. By the late 1960's, the Committee of Supply was sitting for 40 to 60 days each year, providing about 200 hours of study to the Government's expenditure plan.
The pamphlet then goes on to indicate the new system of reference of estimates to committees of the House for detailed scrutiny:
The Committees may, during their examination of the Estimates, call for the appearance of Ministers and departmental officials. They may also call for departmental papers and records to assist them in their examination. If a Committee wishes, it may hear witnesses from outside the Government who possess specialized knowledge and who can assist the Committee to evaluate specific programs.
The happy result of these new steps is this:
By the time the Estimates are reported to the House, the several Standing Committees have spent a total of about 500 hours in studying the Government's expenditure plan. This is more than twice as much time as was spent by the old Committee of Supply.
While the capacity of the House to examine Estimates has been increased, the ancient tradition has been maintained which guarantees members the right to express their grievances in the House of Commons before approving Government spending estimates. A total of 25 days each year is set aside for the Opposition parties to discuss matters of their choosing.
Then, finally:
It is fundamental to the Parliamentary system that the Government's programs be subjected to this detailed and public scrutiny, for it is in this manner that the public is informed each year about differing views on national objectives, and about issues surrounding the means the Government has chosen for achieving these objectives.
I have quoted at some length from this document because I think it describes in plain and simple language the increased capacity of the House to scrutinize the spending plans and programs of the government, and I suggest is a direct refutation of the notion in the motion that, owing to procedural inadequacies, the House has been stifled and its members are being denied the ancient opportunities they allegedly had for questioning, scrutinizing and criticizing the government's programs and spending plans.
On another aspect of this matter, namely the provision of effective information to the House, I made mention of the fact that in 1970 a new form of estimates was introduced to the House of Commons for the first time. This new form of estimates had been the subject of preparation within the government for some period of months, followed by discussion over a great many meetings with the public accounts committee, as a consequence of which some changes in the original government proposals were made, including those proposed by the committee and willingly accepted. This resulted in a new form of the estimates designed to provide more and better information to hon. members concerning the government's proposals for expenditures in the forthcoming year.
On the occasion of the introduction of these proposals, I said, as reported at page 3468 of Hansard for February 11, 1970:
The tabling of these estimates marks a major step forward in an endeavour by the government to improve the process of resource allocation and to better inform Parliament and the people of Canada of the objectives, operations and costs of the departments
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys and agencies of government. The form of these estimates is radically different from that which has been followed for more than half a century. For the first time the expenditure proposals respecting departments and agencies are clearly formulated in terms of programs. The objectives and sub-objectives of each program are stated and the nature of the program further amplified through a description of the activities carried on in pursuit of program objectives.
I then said:
-I believe that the estimates in the form I am now tabling provide a clearer and more informative presentation than we have had heretofore of the proposed allocations of fiscal resources to the budgetary requirements of Canada.
This, then, Mr. Speaker, was another step in improving the ability of parliament to become aware in a meaningful way of the spending proposals of the government and to scrutinize them. I assume from his opening remarks that the hon. member for Peace River has not yet had time to study the new form in which the estimates are now presented. I received the impression from what he said that he was unaware of the change having been made in 1970.
A further measure introduced by the government for improving the capacity of the House effectively to scrutinize government spending programs, plans and policies was the introduction in 1968 of new, hitherto unavailable, research resources for each of the political parties in the House. In that year there was made available to all parties in the House, with the exception, at the outset, of the government party, funds with which to hire persons of the parties' own choosing, reporting only to them, in the field of research into government operations and activities. For the Conservative party, a sum amounting to $125,000 per year was provided; for the New Democratic Party $35,000 per year and an identical sum for the Social Credit party. Some of the remarks I have heard today indicate that these resources are, of course, being used.
It was not until a year later that a comparable sum was provided to members of the House on the government side. This was another measure through which the government endeavoured to improve the capacity of opposition members, indeed of members of the House generally, effectively to examine, scrutinize, and where necessary criticize, the operations, plans, proposals and programs of the government of the day in order to make sure that there is an adequate accounting, through parliament and its members, to the people of Canada.
This morning all members who spoke made reference to an observation in the Auditor General's report, which is the one under discussion here today, about the shortage in the Auditor General's staff and the causes therefor. This has been quite extensively discussed in the House on a previous occasion, and also in the Public Accounts Committee. Unfortunately, the report bears the date of February 29, which ante-dated the examination by the Public Accounts Committee of the current staff position of the Auditor General's office.
After some four meetings during which the Auditor General and myself made statements, the committee reported its conclusions to the House regarding staff shortages as follows:

May 26, 1972
Alleged, Loss of Control of Public Moneys
The Committee has found that Parliament has provided the funds for the number of staff required by the Auditor General. The problem seems to lie in the difficulty of obtaining and retaining qualified staff to fill the approved positions.
The reasons for these difficulties are complex and will require further consideration by the Committee.
It has been suggested by both the President of the Treasury Board and the Auditor General that the solution lies in an Auditor General's Act.
This was the conclusion the committee came to and, as we all know, this was a committee under the chairmanship of a member of that party represented by the official opposition. It came to this conclusion after some considerable time spent on the matter. It would be rather simplistic to assume there were easy and fast solutions which were being withheld on the grounds of ill-will or some other undesirable motive. The committee agreed that the problem was a complex one and that there was no ready solution within the framework of existing legislation. It proposed that an endeavour should be made to find a way around this, under the terms of a new Auditor General's Act, which would serve the principal purpose of ensuring the independence of the office of the Auditor General and provide, hopefully, a solution to this particular problem. Had this particular inquiry by the Public Accounts Committee taken place at an earlier date, before the report which appears to be dated February 29, probably the wording which has been quoted in the press and here by some hon. members today would have taken a rather different form.
This does not alter the fact that there is a problem, or that the office of the Auditor General must be adequately staffed if it is to carry out the important functions with which Parliament has charged that office. We must have funds to obtain staff which is both adequate in numbers and in professional competence. We, on the part of the government, are prepared to do all we can to support that principle. One of the things in this regard is the production of a new act to be known as the Auditor General's act.
Hon. members are fairly familiar with the history of this matter. Some years ago, the government endorsed the suggestion that there should be an Auditor General's act, and that this office should be removed from the ambit of the Financial Administration Act. The willingness and readiness of the government to go the full length desired by Parliament in this respect has been reiterated in this House on a number of occasions by representatives of the government, including myself. Let me make reference to testimony I gave before the Public Accounts Committee on March 16, 1972.1 quote:
Finally the Government has even been prepared to consider exempting the Auditor General entirely from all Treasury Board authority in the matter of budget and staff levels. In April 1970 I said this to the House:
"The Auditor General has made certain proposals which would assure his independence from the normal rules which govern the civil service, thus by inference further affirming his independence of the government. The Government has been prepared to accept the Auditor General's propositions, and indeed to go further than he proposed."
The Government stands by this position, and the alternative which I proposed in 1970 to achieve this end.

I should like to reaffirm that the government will support and encourage the drafting of a new Auditor General's act designed to provide the independence to that office which is essential if the Auditor General is to carry out the functions given to him by Parliament. I am glad to say I have been informed that the Public Accounts Committee, which has been charged by the House with producing legislative proposals in relation to such a bill, has already appointed a sub-committee to initiate the work, and I understand this sub-committee is now at work. I suppose we must recognize here again the fact that, as the Public Accounts Committee earlier found, this is a complex question and one should not anticipate that either the House committee or the sub-committee will be able to solve all the problems in a matter of days or even weeks. However, one looks forward to the occasion when the committee will be able to produce a draft of a bill for presentation to and scrutiny by the House. I trust it will be rather more sympathetically received than the earlier one which was rejected by the official opposition without even an examination of the provisions of the bill itself, or indeed any consideration of the fact that the bill was merely a reflection of the proposals made by the committee, to which the official opposition provides the chairman.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again the Auditor General has drawn attention to the erosion of parliamentary control over the spending powers of Parliament. This type of erosion manifests itself in many ways. It is manifested in the instances cited by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), and I
May 26, 1972

am sure we will hear more as the day progresses. We have heard of one form of erosion of parliamentary control over spending. This was dealt with by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in his speech of Monday, May 15, in which he drew attention to the increases in the income tax rate structure and allowances. It is to the control Parliament has over spending, particularly as this relates to the new rules affecting committees, that I wish to address my remarks this afternoon.
We have heard a good deal about reform of the rules of the House. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) referred to the changes. This process of reform, which culminated in the changes of 1968, followed a study of the rules of the House by a Special Committee on Procedure. As a result of that study, the committees of the House were to assume a new and important function. That function arose largely from the fact that committees, as a consequence of the rule changes, would examine all legislation, with the exception of tax bills, and would examine all of the spending estimates of the House instead of this being done in the committee of the whole house which carried out this function before the rule changes.
There are 18 committees of the House. Most of these committees have the responsibility of examining spending estimates. The third report of the Special Committee on Procedure of 1968 expressed the hope that the reports of standing committees would assume a critical significance related more closely to the national interest as a whole than to simple political differences. The procedure Committee hoped as well that debate in the standing committees would be well informed and pertinent, and that their members would become influential in the areas of their specialized expertise. Unfortunately, that expectation has not been realized because the same rule changes which ended the power of the committee of the whole to examine spending estimates, also strangled the standing committees by rules which, to my mind, make examination of estimates totally ineffective and at best a frustrating exercise.
The main weakness of the new rules, so far as the responsibility of committees to handle spending estimates is concerned, is cited in paragraph 14 of Standing Order 58 which reads:
In every session the main estimates to cover the incoming fiscal year for every department of government shall be referred to standing committees on or before March 1 of the then expiring fiscal year. Each such committee shall consider and shall report, or shall be deemed to have reported, the same back to the House not later than May 31 in the then current fiscal year.
Well, what that means, in effect, is that regardless of how many meetings the committees may have in the course of the examination of their estimates, and regardless of how many witnesses the committees may call in examining the estimates of the department before them, it is all a useless exercise because all of the estimates will be deemed to have been reported back to the House and passed by May 31 each year.
In reflecting on the workings of the committees of this Parliament, one might have the impression that the new rules are working well. For instance, it is interesting to note that in the first session of the present Parliament, 520 hours and 22 minutes were spent on examination of esti-
Alleged. Loss of Control of Public Moneys mates. In the second session of this Parliament about the same time was spent on estimates. In the third session a total of 229 hours and 54 minutes were spent on the examination of the main estimates, plus another 43 hours and 46 minutes on supplementary estimates. In the fourth session, to date as of May 19, 195 hours and 47 minutes, plus 15 hours and 43 minutes were spent on estimates and supplementary estimates. This may seem like an impressive record until one examines the day-by-day workings of the committees.
First of all, a very dangerous practice has crept into the committee system, which I believe is illegal, whereby committees under the same rule changes which were brought in in 1968 are now permitted to sit and hear evidence without a quorum. This means that not more than half a dozen members, if indeed that many, were present during the majority of the time in which the committees studied and examined the estimates. Most of the committees have adopted a procedure, in order to get around this contradictory provision in the rules, which stipulates that at least five members be in attendance with at least one member from each of the main opposition parties. This, however, does not always work. Quite frankly, I find difficulty in understanding how a committee, which is supposed to be a microcosm of this House and which is supposed to reflect the rules and procedures of this House, can legally sit, conduct its hearing, hear witnesses and have all the paraphernalia for the recording and transcribing of evidence without having a quorum, because the committee would really not be legally in session. Most of the committees of the House require at least 11 members for a quorum. As if that were not bad enough, the new rule change to my mind makes the whole committee system a farce because it totally denies and eliminates any suggestion that the committee develop a spirit of collegiality and expertise in its particular field.
I refer to Standing Order 65(4)(b) which reads:
Changes in the membership of any standing, joint or special committee may be effected by a notification thereof, signed by the member acting as the Chief Government Whip, being filed with the Clerk of the House who shall cause the same to be printed in the Votes and Proceedings of the House of that sitting, or of the next sitting thereafter, as the case may be.
But here is one rule that is abused. It should never have been placed there in the first instance, because now the government whips can, by use of their majority, replace members on committees from time to time without any notification. They can move in roving squads to bolster their majority on committees as the need may arise. These squads, which roam around from committee to committee, generally know little or nothing of what has been going on in the committee. Their sole function is to carry out the wish of the government majority, to ensure that the government majority functions in the committee, and to thwart the legitimate efforts of the committee members to study, to reach a conclusion and a resolution as a consequence of these studies. Is it any wonder, then, that the attendance in the standing committees of the House is so dismally low? Is it any wonder that the committees of the House meet with only four or five members present? I attended two committee meetings yesterday, and at no
2604

May 26, 1972
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys time during the course of these meetings when estimates were being examined was there a quorum present.
Then, we have the scheduling of the committee meetings, which again defeats the very purpose of the system because a number of government departments are being examined in committees at the same time. This denies members of the House the right, and indeed the responsibility they have, to examine the estimates of the government. A random sampling of the Votes and Proceedings of the day indicates that next Tuesday six committees are scheduled to meet: the Committee on Agriculture, the Committee on Broadcasting, the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, the Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, the Committee on National Resources and Public Works and the Committee on Regional Development. How can any member of the House conscientiously discharge his duties, be present and examine the estimates of the departments or present his grievances or indeed examine legislation when perhaps all of these committees are meeting at the same time?
It is not difficult to understand why the government invokes the use of Standing Order 65(4)(b), because without it they could not man the committees themselves. Too many committees meet at any given time, and there are not enough members at any given time to man them. There you see an example of the very concept of the new committee system-that is the concept of expertise in our related fields plus the concept of collegiality-being thwarted and defeated by these rules. Regardless of the rules, and regardless of what the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) may have to say, nothing that we as opposition members may say or do in committees will influence one single, solitary cent of government expenditures-

I make no exceptions. It is no wonder that the members of this House are becoming cynical and lethargic with respect to their duties in the House because in fact, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said, we are practically nobodies. He said we are nobodies when the House closes, so we are practically nobodies when the House is in session because, although we are here, we have no power over government spending. Members of the opposition have lost their traditional responsibility to control government spending, and indeed the members of the government party who have traditionally had the responsibility of manning committees and being, like the official opposition, watchdogs of the public purse, have become cynical.

Mr. Speaker, the motion we have before us, put forward by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), to me is like going elephant hunting with a flyswatter. I think clearly there are things that people might well complain about in respect of the observations of the Auditor General of Canada, but the motion before us does not touch in any way upon any of those issues. In my view this motion only brings to the attention of Parliament something that the Auditor General has commented upon, and which does not constitute any act of illegality on the part of the executive. I say this for a very good reason. The matter of Parliamentary control has been discussed at considerable length in the Public Accounts committee, and I would like to deal with the question in very specific terms.
The motion before us indicates that the government has evaded its constitutional responsibility and certain legal safeguards by allowing money to be carried over from one fiscal year to the next. It is suggested that there is something wrong in doing this, and that this parliamentary institution is opposed to this practice. As a basis for that statement, the Financial Administration Act is quoted. The Financial Administration Act is also quoted in the Auditor General's report, in particular section 20, but in case some people happen to take that report too literally I want to draw attention to the fact that it is not

May 26, 1972
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys section 20 but section 25 of the act which prohibits these moneys from being carried over from one year to the next.
My understanding of the law is that parliament is supreme, and that a specific act of parliament takes precedence over a general act of parliament. Upon that basis, I would like to review some of the specific observations that have been made. For example, vote L55 for the CBC is described as "Loans on terms and conditions approved by the Governor in council to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the current and subsequent fiscal years for capital expenditures." A sum of $25 million is provided. This vote, approved by Parliament, rightly or wrongly, is an expenditure which could in fact by law be carried over to some subsequent year. If parliament has made a mistake, it is parliament's responsibility to say so, and correct it if it so chooses. However I do not find it-and I say this with all respect-within the purview of the Auditor General of Canada to say, as in effect he is saying, that parliament has made a mistake in approving that kind of estimate. If it did make a mistake this type of reflection on parliament should come from parliamentarians themselves.
The same thing applies to other estimates to which reference has been made, and so far as I know to all the estimates referred to in connection with the carrying over of expenditures. For instance vote L25 for the Canadian International Development Agency in the sum of $150 million clearly spells out that this money is for use in the current and subsequent fiscal years. Again, it is clear that parliament agreed to that particular approach. We can hardly blame the executive for acting upon the approval that was given to it by parliament itself.
The same is true, and in a more glaring way, with respect to vote 75 in the estimates of the Department of Transport. This is also cited in the Auditor General's report when he refers to money granted to the National Harbours Board. The vote here of $1,200,000 clearly indicates that this is the amount to be credited to the National Harbours Board special account, and is to constitute an absolute grant without interest. One can hardly blame the National Harbours Board for treating it as a grant when it clearly was a grant, and I presume if it was a grant that it was one without strings attached. One can hardly blame the executive for treating it as parliament said it should be treated.
One could go on and on. Vote No. 5 was discussed at length in the Public Accounts Committee because it is a provision whereby the Treasury Board sets aside moneys to look after retroactive pay increases that may be granted as a result of the unionization of public employees. This money is granted on an annual basis and carries with it, according to the vote, the right to carry that fund over for payment as a charge in the year in which it is granted. That is quite clear as far as the wording of the estimates are concerned.
On a number of occasions in the Public Accounts Committee I have stated that it may well be that Parliament does not know what it is doing, but one can hardly blame the executive for the stupidity of people in this House who

now complain that we are doing what they authorized us to do. I do not know that it is the function of the Auditor General or anyone else to take members of this House by the hand and walk them through the estimates saying, "Gentlemen, you ought to know what you are doing before you vote." Clearly members ought to study these matters beforehand. It seems to me that the opposition might be able to tap some of the resource facilities given by this government in order to look into these matters in depth and express their objections, if they have any, at the time the estimates are discussed.
