May I put some facts on record that may be of edification to the hon. member. They have to do with government expenditures. We shall see whether they were authorized by Parliament or not. Let me cite one example for the hon. member. He may examine it and derive benefit from it. The net total of accepted incentive grants under the Regional Development Incentives Act to the end of 1971-72 fiscal year was estimated to be $233,301,493 according to the summary tabled by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) on April 13, 1972. By that date, however, only $60 million or $70 million had actually been paid out. This means that DREE had entered into agreements with companies which would lead to expenditures of about $165 million beyond those approved by Parliament to that date.
According to the latest RDIA summary, the estimated value of accepted offers had risen to $250,110,024 by the end of April. According to information tabled by the DREE deputy minister, RDIA expenditures contained in the 1972-73 estimates would amount to about $125 million. Commitments to firms have thus already been made which exceed by about $50 million even the amounts contained in the estimates up to the end of March, 1973. The foregoing, Mr. Speaker, is an example of the government spending money that it had no authority to spend.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) dealt with two aspects of the Auditor General's report. I wish to deal with a third aspect, the spending of taxpayers' money, as outlined in the Auditor General's report, that has caused great damage. That money was spent without authority and in an incompetent manner; the government violated the trust given to it by the people of Canada.
Shocking revelations were made by the Auditor General, especially in the Department of National Defence, which lead to the inescapable conclusion that that department among the 27 departments of government leads the list by a country mile as the most glaringly incompetent, wasteful and inexcusably inefficiently run department in Canada. The excess of its collective incompetence almost requires a special auditor general to supervise its operations. Even worse than its operations are its decisions in the DDH program, the CF-5 procurement program and the mothballing of the hydrofoil Bras d'Or.
The gross incompetence of the department's decisionmaking and the magnitude of its blunders in these three spheres requires that action be taken by the government of Canada to determine exactly who is responsible for the incompetence. Is it the minister, the deputy minister and his officials; is it the chiefs of staff of this country or is it a combination of all three? Surely someone ought to be answerable to the people of Canada for the extravagant waste of money which has occurred year after year in that department. I do not know how much longer the people of Canada can be asked to put up with such incompetence.
May 26, 1972

Year after year the Auditor General presents his report, and year after year we see the catalogue of errors committed by the Department of National Defence. We have reached the point where a committee of this House has censured the officials of the department, yet the government has done nothing.
One would have thought that after the financial fiasco associated with the Bonaventure we could have expected an end to the type of incompetence and extravagance associated with Department of National Defence programs. But no; again in this year's Auditor General's report we have another catalogue of mistakes, failures and desperate estimates of costs of programs. There is an absolute and incomplete indifference on the part of the government and the Department of National Defence to do anything about the gross incompetence associated with the department.
I would like to give some specific instances of this incompetence. One is the destroyer deployment helicopter program. In 1966 we were told that this program was estimated to cost $145 million. In 1967 the cost had risen to $165 million, in 1967-68 to $192 million, in 1970 to $225 million, in 1971 to $252 million, in 1971-72 to $282 million and today we are told the estimate could run as high as $330 million. It has risen from $145 million to $330 million-and what do we get from the government? We do not get anything in the way of a reasonable explanation for the tremendous escalation in costs which the taxpayer is paying. This government goes blandly on its way with no apparent concern about the escalation in cost. This escalation in cost does not involve the helicopters that will be associated with destroyers. At the very minimum there will be eight helicopters, probably more. They each cost in the vicinity of $2 million; therefore you can add another $16 million to the estimate of $330 million.
The time has come for the question of Department of National Defence and the way it is run to be taken out of the hands of the Auditor General and placed in the hands of a special committee. I think the best group of individuals to do the job would be a committee of the other place. They have been able to examine many areas and various institutions in this country, how they operate, and what they do and whether they do it properly. They could make a determination of who is responsible for the incompetence associated with the revelations that have been provided year after year by the Auditor General.
It is obvious that this government pays no attention to the Auditor General. Year after year he tells the government the same story and they allow the same things to happen. No matter what the government is told by what organization, they allow the department to go on its merry way and make decisions that have no degree of sense, such as the hydrofoil program.
The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. For-restall) pointed out to the government on numerous occasions, even before the Auditor General's report was made public, that these things were happening in the department. Surely some corrective action could have been taken by the government during that period, but nothing has been done. The record shows that the hon. member
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys for Dartmouth-Halifax East has made the government aware of the scandalous errors in judgment within the Department of National Defence and the Department of Supply and Services regarding the destroyer deployment helicopter program.
Let us turn to the hydrofoil program. The Auditor General said in his report:
Expenditure to May 31, 1971, totalled $51.1 million including $444,000 for the replacement of a foil which cracked during trials in mid-1969, in respect of which the Department of Supply and Services later concluded that it had no claim against the contractor. In October 1971 the Treasury Board approved an increase of $1 million to place and maintain the hydrofoil in a state of preservation from which it may be reactivated within the next five years, bringing the approved cost of the program to $53.2 million.
If this program was not going to be followed through by the government, it should have been killed a long time before $53.2 million was spent on it. When it reached the point where Canada had produced the fastest ship in the world, tested it, proven it to manoeuvre and do what modern warfare requires of a ship, the government should have carried through and concluded the program.
If the Bras D'Or were in operation today we would have much less trouble on the east coast with Russian trawlers moving into our territorial waters and interfering with our fishery. Surely the Bras D'Or could have been useful, outside of national defence purposes, on both the east and west coasts of Canada. What we have now is $53 million in mothballs. By the time the five years are up, the Department of National Defence will probably determine that it will be cheaper to scrap this hydrofoil and build a new one.
That is the sort of decision we have been constantly getting from the Department of National Defence. The time has come for that department to be examined in depth by independent people in order to determine who is responsible for the gross in competence so that the Canadian taxpayer has knowledge of who is continuously wasting his money. We have exactly the same type of story with the CF-5 program. There is no difference at all.
I now wish to turn to comments made by the Auditor General with regard to the guaranteed income supplement and a totally unrelated matter, concessions made to motor vehicle manufacturers, particularly the concession made to one manufacturer which I believe was in the neighbourhood of $6.3 million because that manufacturer did not come within the meaning of the Canada-U.S. auto agreement. As far as the guaranteed income supplement is concerned, the Auditor General said:
The five per cent check made by the Department of National Health and Welfare in 1971 of 1970 income suggests that the annual overpayment may now have reached a total in excess of $9 million. On December 7, 1971, the Public Accounts Committee was advised that the check to be made in 1972 of 1971 income was being increased to ten per cent.
That means that twice as many public servants will be investigating, in effect, the old age pensioners of this country. For some time the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) has been making effort after effort to find out why the Department of National Health and Welfare has been garnisheeing old age pension cheques in order to recover overpayments made to them. The hon. member
2610

May 26, 1972
Alleged Loss of Control o f Public Moneys has been frustated because the minister will not answer his questions in the House.
What frustrates me and other members of the House is that we have discovered that most of the mistakes made on the cheques are not the result of misinformation or fraudulent information on the part of the recipients but miscalculations of staff of the Department of National Health and Welfare who have overestimated the payment a pensioner should receive. On discovering that an individual has been overpaid in this way, the department proceeds to garnishee his pension cheques for some time in order to recover the overpayment, which as I say has resulted from a mistake made by a departmental official.
Most of the cases that have come to my attention indicate that the mistakes were initially made by departmental officials, not by the recipients of the cheques. If the pensioner is in receipt of the guaranteed income supplement, then he is living on an income well below the poverty line. The department then tell such an individual that they are going to reduce even that minimum income because somebody in the office made a mistake and paid him too much. Whatever this individual receives in his cheque was needed by him because it was all he had to live on, yet the government reduces his payment to below that provided by the legislation, because one of its staff made a mistake that must be corrected.
When the government discovers that an automobile manufacturer in this country cannot qualify under the Canada-United States auto agreement, the government has no problem at all in forgiving the company $6.3 million that it owes the government. But the story is quite different if you are not a big automobile manufacturer but a poor individual. I contend that if such a mistake occurs through no fault of the recipient, the error should be forgiven in exactly the same way that the automobile manufacturer to whom I have referred was forgiven $6.3 million. What is good enough for an automobile manufacturer should be good enough for individual Canadians, especially those who are asked to subsist on old age security and the guaranteed income supplement.
I should now like to deal with another matter. It is a wonderful thing that this country does have an Auditor General. The hon. member for St. John's East pointed out during his speech ways in which Members of Parliament have been unable to get information that they require and to which they have the right. About 18 months ago I put a question on the order paper asking how much language training was costing the people of Canada. I put the question in a number of specific ways. One of the questions I asked was whether or not included in the cost of language training was the cost to the government of the period during which people taking language training were away from their jobs.

In any case, he mentioned the difficulties that the Auditor General seemed to have in the staffing of his office and this has been for years the subject of debates that have gone on and on endlessly on this method of staffing. As late as last March, then, we were hopeful that once and for all we could deal with this question and settle the problem. On a motion from the Conservative party, we would have tried to hear the Audi-
May 26, 1972

tor General and the President of the Treasury Board to settle the question, to determine whether there was any possibility of improving the situation and to see who was responsible for staffing, how to retain the staff, and why the staff was leaving that office.
In answer to the question put to him on March 14 last, the Auditor General said that he wanted to specify to the members of the committee that he himself was preparing the credits for the staff to be recruited for the coming twelve months, and that he was entrusting the recruiting to the Civil Service Commission.
So the President of the Treasury Board has nothing to do with the recruiting of personnel, nor has the government any responsibility in that regard. But the fact remains that the Auditor General repeated again that recruiting was difficult because of conditions that were never made clear.
Mr. Speaker, it was noted at that time that civil servants had left the service of the Auditor General for undetermined reasons, and that failure to keep them had not only jeopardized the efficiency of his office but has also delayed preparation of his report.
We have tried to determine if those who had resigned were grade 4 or 5 employees, that is those who have heavier responsibilities than others and we have found out that 28 employees who had effectively resigned-some 30 persons had been mentioned-had less than two or three years of service and that among those who had several years of service, apparently only one had reached 20 years.
We have tried to determine whether there would not be some other procedure to improve the hiring of personnel but according to the information obtained, it seems that the employees are not so eager to work within a restricted field, namely the Auditor General's office and this for several reasons. One of the most obvious reasons is that there are fewer opportunities for promotion within a small office, while public servants are working in a much more extensive organization with 5,000 or 6,000 employees.
The acquired rights of these officials are for them very precious elements, and they are certainly very reluctant to remain, let us say, confined in a much more restricted service than the Public Service offers them. And naturally, promotion opportunities, in such a limited organization, are fewer and slower. People must show much more patience in order to get promotion or progress in their work.
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to deal a little with certain paragraphs that we find in the Auditor General's report, which has only been tabled early this week, and that the members of the House or those of the Committee on Public Accounts have not had yet time to examine.
But there are a couple of paragraphs that I would like to deal with, Mr. Speaker, and I think particularly of paragraph 142 which deals with frauds committed by people who are drawing old age security benefits. And I am sure that the term used is not the proper one.
During the examination of the 1969-70 report, we brought to the attention of the Auditor General the term "fraud" used to designate these amounts which had been
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys paid to the people receiving unsolicited benefits. These amounts, obtained in an unpremeditated way and without the intention of defrauding the government, must be reimbursed. Paragraph 142 indicates that, out of a total of $1,039,000 accumulated over the past few years, $532,000 have been reimbursed to the federal government.
Sometimes, for one reason or another, a change may occur in the social condition of a person receiving benefits and render him ineligible to benefits. Then, when these overpayments are discovered, some time naturally elapses before the full amount owed is duly reimbursed.
Again, Mr. Speaker, we strongly object to the use of the term "fraud" when no fraud has been proved and notwithstanding a few possible cases of fraud I really feel that we should rather admire the honesty of the majority of Canadians who receive these payments.
Mr. Speaker, before closing I should also like to call the attention of hon. members to another paragraph, No. 124, dealing specifically with the setting aside of CF5 aircraft, the cost thereof to the Canadian government and the amounts that could have been saved by converting these aircraft, this equipment from bomber and observation aircraft to trainers.
There is a mention of an amount of $5 million which could have been saved. When aircraft of the CF5 type are designed for a very specific role, it is impossible for the Canadian government, the Department of National Defense to convert them economically into trainers because, since they were not designed for this role, the cost of conversion could considerably exceed the cost to the government of purchasing trainer aircraft instead.
This is therefore another paragraph which will certainly receive careful study and examination by members of the Public Accounts Committee.
Mr. Speaker, that will conclude my remarks.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED EROSION OF PARLIAMENT'S CONTROL OVER GOVERNMENT SPENDING AS A RESULT OF EVASION OF CONSTITUTIONAL SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, each year the Auditor General presents a report of considerable length containing numerous examples of improper use of public funds, inefficiencies and waste; and each year we in the opposition and those in the news media with much glee and gusto draw the attention of the public to the faults, foibles and worse perpetrated by public servants as revealed by the Auditor General's report. The government of the day is quite correctly held responsible for the waste the Auditor General reveals and almost invariably suffers politically as a result for a short time.
This annual exercise has by now almost become a spring ritual. It is useful despite this fact, because it encourages governments to be much more vigilant in their supervision of the expenditure of public funds than they otherwise might be in order to avoid as much opprobrium and ridicule as possible. However, with the exception of this case the annual spring ritual to me would seem to be largely beside the point.
The role of the Auditor General, as an officer of Parliament, is to provide parliamentarians with the expert assistance necessary to properly supervise government
2612

May 26, 1972
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys expenditures. Public servants are human; they will commit their share of errors, follies and stupidities. Occasionally, and it is a tribute to the Public Sevice of Canada that the occasions are very rare, there will even be outright dishonesty. Governments, too, are composed of human beings who will seek ways and means to juggle accounts so as to make their performance seem just a bit better than it actually is. Thus, I believe that the most important function of the annual report of the Auditor General is not so much that of pointing out past errors as that of indicating how similar errors may be avoided in the future.
It is in that light that I say the most damning indictment of the government contained in this year's report is that the government has refused to act on a total of 38 recommendations, 31 by the Auditor General and seven by the Public Accounts Committee which were designed to increase government efficiency and to enhance the effectiveness of parliamentary supervision of the expenditure of public funds. Here the government was provided with expert, well considered and dispassionate advice on how to make better use of the tax dollar, and the government has chosen to ignore it.
Mistakes in public expenditure are always to be regretted and every attempt must be made to eliminate them. But because we are human beings, subject to error, we can forgive them. What I cannot forgive is a government's deliberate neglect of opportunities to reduce waste and error. This government, through the recommendations of the Auditor General's reports and the recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee, was provided with a golden opportunity to reduce waste and error in the use of the tax dollar and it chose to ignore that opportunity. That is unforgiveable.
My other major concern which arises out of this year's report of the Auditor General is the solid information it provides which indicates that parliamentary as opposed to governmental supervision of public expenditure remains woefully inadequate. Funds in massive amounts have even been spent in ways not authorized by Parliament.

speechtext:
Pass over the report and I will cite the examples. Parliament traditionally serves three functions, the formation of policy, the raising of revenue for the purpose of implementing public policy and the supervision of the expenditure of the tax dollar. For various reasons, too well known to be gone into here, we can no longer expect the legislature to carry nearly as much weight as the executive or cabinet in the first two areas of policy formation and the raising of revenue. But surely it is legitimate to expect that the legislature do yoeman service in the supervision of government expenditures,

and surely it is mandatory that every facility be provided for the efficient fulfilment by the legislature of its role in this regard.
Many suggestions for the accomplishment of this goal are contained in the neglected recommendations of the Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee to which I have already referred. I would like to make three more suggestions. The first suggestion arises out of the fact that many government programs are now of such a nature that they involve commitments for expenditure in future years which must be honoured but which Parliament has no opportunity to examine in detail in advance or at the time of commitment. To be more specific, cash grants offered to private companies under the Regional Development Incentives Act are spread over a number of years. Certain amounts are paid out over a four or five-year period. Consequently, departmental expenditures on incentives in a given year, which are voted by Parliament, consist of two kinds: first, payments to companies on behalf of arrangements made in this same year; second, payments to companies under contractual arrangements made a year or two or three years before-contractual arrangements which Parliament is hardly in a position to repudiate.
The present system does not permit Parliament to exercise any control over this situation. Only a multi-year budgetary system could handle it. Alternatively, in recognition of the fact that we will not be getting the multi-year budgetary system, Parliament has the right to know what commitments are incurred by departments for future years. For example, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has been refusing to reveal its commitments to companies for future fiscal years. It should be forced by Parliament to disclose that information, not only for the sake of the parliamentary process but for the sake of the Treasury Board in its attempts to justify the expenditure of public funds.
In fact, looking at the accelerated pace of DREE grants, especially in the last 12 months, expenditures in future years will escalate rapidly. It is estimated that at the present pace, in five years time the commitments may reach $1 billion annually. Does Parliament want that kind of expenditure, and indeed does government want it? Surely an opportunity must be given Parliament, through the devices I have suggested or through some closely allied approach, to answer these questions about DREE and indeed about other departments which are involved in programs requiring the commitment of funds for years in advance.
My second suggestion is that to complete the circle of Parliamentary supervision of expenditures, the Comptroller General should cease to be a public servant in the orthodox sense and become, rather, an officer of Parliament as is the Auditor General. The current, well defined division of duties between the Auditor General and the comptroller must be applauded. However, there would seem to be a curious lack of logic in not making the Comptroller General an independent officer of Parliament as is the Auditor General.
The comptroller's task is, after all, in the words of Norman Ward, "in essence to ensure that all money is spent as Parliament said it should be, in no larger
May 26, 1972

amounts and for no other purposes than Parliament approved." Computers, as the Glassco commission pointed out, have virtually eliminated the comptroller's actual accounting duties. The fact that the comptroller is not an officer of Parliament means that there is a break in the circle of parliamentary control of finance, a break which did not occur prior to 1931 when the Auditor General carried out a pre-audit of government expenditures as well as a post-audit as he does today.
The Auditor General may of course, and he does, include references to breaches of parliamentary instructions in his annual report. Such references have value but they are always after the fact; the discovery is always made when it is too late to do anything about it. An independent comptroller could challenge on the spot and force a ruling. The method of adjudicating potential disputes between the cabinet or the executive and the comptroller could be so established as to do no violence to the principle that the government alone is responsible for the use of funds. For example, the Minister of Justice could be made the arbitrator in disputes between the comptroller and the Treasury Board. The minister's decision would be final, thus ensuring no interruption of the operations of government, but subject to scrutiny and reversal by Parliament. Any such disputes, together with the decision of the Minister of Justice, could immediately be placed before Parliament and/or one of its committees, perhaps the public Accounts Committee, for consideration and report.
I am somewhat loth to begin an explanation of my third suggestion for improved parliamentary control over finances; it requires considerably more detailed presentation, in order to be fully understood, than the time available to me permits. But I will make a stab at it. I think Parliament needs to recreate a standing committee on estimates, not with a view to replacing the present practice of departmental estimates being referred to appropriate standing committees but with the idea of supplementing that practice. It would not be expected that such a committee would examine the estimates of all departments in a single year but, rather, go into detail with respect to a few departments each year with the hope perhaps of covering each department during the life of a Parliament.
On the surface, that may seem to be a useless duplication of effort already being made by existing standing committees, but a close examination will demonstrate that such is not the case. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) devoted considerable attention to the shortcomings of our committee system with respect to the examination of estimates and I do not intend to repeat his arguments. The point I wish to make is that the customary practice in committees dealing with estimates is to question only those items which are increased or decreased drastically in any one year. Professor Hockin suggested as follows:
-this high-spotting of the estimates fosters a delusive sense of task fulfilment. It is based upon the Burkean fallacy that what is changed is worth scrutiny, what remains the same is not.
That is certainly not a principle which can be followed when examining government expenditures in order to
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys determine the wisdom of those expenditures, because it is notorious that governments continue programs long after they become redundant. I am arguing that for Parliament to properly supervise finances, expertise among Members of Parliament of the business-budget analysis sort must be created. Because of other demands on their time, existing standing committees are unlikely to develop that kind of expertise.
I envisage an estimates committee as having the time and the single-minded purpose to devote time to developing some fairly concise concepts of the proper principles which should be employed to govern expenditures. Such a committee should devise a method of detailed and, more importantly, systematic examination of all estimates submitted to it. One of the main purposes of such an examination would be to reveal any breach of the principles governing expenditures which the committee has devised.
Such a committee should also formulate general and specific recommendations for the form in which main estimates are presented, in order to ensure that they can be easily understood by a layman, which most Members of Parliament are when it comes to looking at balance sheets, and to ensure that they facilitate parliamentary control over governmental expenditures. I could go on listing tasks which an estimates committee might usefully perform, but my over-all purpose is clear. It is to create expertise in the kinds of principles necessary to properly control government expenditures, exper tise which at present does not exist or if it does exist, does so in only isolated circumstances.
Obviously, some overlap would be involved with the tasks of the Public Accounts Committee. Liaison between the two committees would thus be desirable and it could be accomplished, I suggest, by adopting the British practice of making the chairman of each of the two committees ex officio a member of the other and by having the comptroller and Auditor General available to each committee. Those are my three suggestions: a means of controlling commitments for future expenditure made possible by legislation but not requiring simultaneous parliamentary approval, making the Comptroller General an officer of Parliament, and creating a standing committee on estimates.
I hope hon. members will give the ideas some consideration because even though they might not in themselves provide all the answers it is obvious, on the basis of this year's Auditor General's report, that parliamentary supervision of government expenditures is totally inadequate; and if Parliament is to be a meaningful institution devices must be discovered quickly to improve that supervision.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED EROSION OF PARLIAMENT'S CONTROL OVER GOVERNMENT SPENDING AS A RESULT OF EVASION OF CONSTITUTIONAL SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the mover insinuates that Parliament's control over government spending of public funds has decreased in the last few years, and this, for various reasons. I believe the contrary is true and I should like to quote certain facts in support of my assertion.
Since 1968, all government expenditures have been referred to one or another of the 16 standing committees of the House. This allows the committee members-and

May 26, 1972
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys on this point I disagree with the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath)-to perform efficient work. This also enables them not only to question the ministers responsible for the various departments, but also their officials as well, and if they so desire, witnesses from the private sector, a practice which would be impossible if we still followed the former procedure of studying government expenditures in Committee of the Whole.
Mr. Speaker, referring to a study made by the Committees Branch, I see that during the second session of the 28th Parliament, 152 meetings were spent on the study of the various departmental estimates.
For the 4th session of the 28th Parliament, to May 25, 1972, 124 meetings were devoted to the study of various departmental estimates.
Over and above the committees which study estimates, we also have to consider the mechanism for checking expenses, which is the public accounts committee. This committee again considered the matter of checking public accounts last fall, on November 9 and 16, 1971, as is evidence in Issues Nos. 51 and 52 of the committee proceedings. On that occasion, the committee had the pleasure of hearing Mr. Balls, assistant deputy minister of the Department of Supply and Services, who informed us that as far as tabling public accounts for the year 1970-71 was concerned, the government had made a commitment, back in 1968, through the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Richardson), to table the Public Accounts of Canada on October 31 at the latest. This year, the three volumes were tabled, the last of which on November 4, 1971.
The Public Accounts Committee set up a sub-committee made up of a member from each party and representatives for the Auditor General, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Supply and Services, to make a study in depth of the possibility of accelerating the tabling in the House of the public accounts of Canada.
Since 1968, as a result of the recommendation of the government, the Canadian Parliament has allotted funds to the opposition parties to retain the services of support personnel. The funds are allotted annually as follows: to the Progressive Conservative party, $125,000; to the New Democratic party, $35,000, and to the Social Credit Party of Canada, $35,000.
The Standing Orders of the House afford the opposition parties other opportunities to study the various departmental estimates. I "refer here to Standing Order 58(3), and I quote:
(3) Opposition motions on allotted days may be moved only by members in opposition to the government and may relate to any matter within the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada and also may be used for the purpose of considering reports from standing committees relating to the consideration of estimates therein.
I will also quote subsection (5) of Standing Order 58:
(5) For the period ending not later than December 10, five sitting days shall be allotted to the business of supply. Seven additional days shall be allotted to the business of supply in the period ending not later than March 26. Thirteen additional days shall be allotted to the business of supply in the period ending not later than June 30.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, 25 days are allotted to the opposition.

I think the formula which consists in referring the study of government expenses to standing committees and, once those expenses have been made, to give them to the public accounts committee to consider, is a very satisfactory and very effective formula.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said in his remarks on this motion that the government was unduly delaying consideration of the Auditor General's report.
Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General's report for the financial year ended March 31, 1970, was tabled in this House on June 4, 1971, and the House adjourned for the summer recess on June 30, 1971. The House reconvened on September 7, 1971, and on September 29 of that same year, it referred the Auditor General's report to the public accounts committee.
The committee started consideration of the report on October 14, 1971, held 17 meetings, and is now preparing its report.
Mr. Speaker, I will leave hon. members to decide whether the government unduly delayed consideration of the Auditor General's report.

A tabulation of these 38 recommendations indicates that the government has indeed responded to them, although not necessarily by acting in the fashion proposed. A substantial number of the issues have been subject to hearings before the Public Accounts Committee. I may say that in most cases these have satisfied the committee, because the subsequent reports of the committee have not raised the issues again.
I now refer to tabulations of issues and action taken. Many of these have been subject to lengthy debate. In this regard the committee has played an effective role and the procedure is not as ineffective as indicated. Mr. Speaker, the following is a summary of action taken on recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee: First, recommendations on which there has been specific comment by the minister involved, 14; second, recommendations on which there has been subsequent specific testimony by departments to the Public Accounts Committee without any new or changed recommendation by the committee, eight; third, recommendations on which departments have not been called upon to testify to the Public Accounts Committee but on which they have taken action which has not received publicity, three; fourth, recommendations which call for continued observation by the Auditor General of departmental practices rather than government action, one; fifth, recommendations subject to action re formulation of separate Auditor General Act, one; sixth, action could not be determined in time avail-
May 26, 1972

able since tabling of Auditor General's report, four; seventh, recommendations made too recently for action to be taken, seven. This makes a total of 38.
I will now list recommendations on which there has been specific comment by the minister involved. In regard to assistance to provinces by armed forces, the Auditor General's 1971 report states advice was given to the House by the Minister of National Defence in September, 1971, and by the Prime Minister in October 1971 of action taken by the government. Regarding indirect compensation to chartered banks, the Auditor General's report states that the Minister of Finance wrote the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee outlining the views of the department but the committee has not given consideration to these views.
In respect of awards under the Pension Act, the minister wrote the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, January 17, 1972. On war veterans allowances the minister wrote the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee on January 17, 1972.
Then there are the following items: amendments to Customs Act and Excise Tax Act; possible loss of revenue when goods lose tax-exempt status; drawback paid on goods destroyed after release from Customs; tax exemptions for particular groups. In these respects the minister wrote the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee on April 20, 1972.
With respect to the audit of office of the Auditor General, the Minister of Finance wrote the Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee on January 26, 1967. The President of the Treasury Board confirmed this to the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee on December 9, 1971. Regarding the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, the Minister of Finance wrote the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee on January 26, 1967. On the cost of abandoned design plans the minister answered to the transport committee on May 25, 1972, which was yesterday.
As to parliamentary control of expenditures, the Auditor General's 1971 report states the President of the Treasury Board in December, 1971, informed the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee that the board was unable to see how its practices, sanctioned by parliament, weakened parliamentary control over expenditures. On the question of excessive advance payments under contracts, the President of the Treasury Board wrote the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee on December 9, 1971. Concerning delay in collecting sales tax, the Auditor General's 1971 report states that the minister advised the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee on November 25, 1970, that amendment to legislation forms part of department's legislative program.
I will now refer to recommendations on which there has been subsequent specific testimony by departments to the Public Accounts Committee without any new or changed recommendation by the committee: second-class mail- testimony March 11 and March 16, 1971; governor general's special warrants-testimony May 18, 1971; errors in Public Service Superannuation Act-testimony April 27, 1971; interest charges on loans to NCC-testimony May 6, 1971; loans and advances representing grants to Crown corporations-testimony May 6, 1971.

Then we have reconstitution of financial structure of National Harbours Board-Auditor General's report states that the Public Accounts Committee discussed the matter on May 13, 1971, with the National Harbours Board and Canadian maritime transportation administration, but no further recommendation has been made by the committee; co-ordination of research and development to industry-testimony November 4, 1971; provision of navigational aids without charge to users-department reported to Public Accounts Committee May 25, 1971, that it was negotiating overflight charges with the International Air Transportation Association.
I will continue, Mr. Speaker, because it was said by at least two hon. members that nothing was done with respect to the 38 recommendations of the Public Accounts Committee. I deal now with recommendations on which departments have not been called to testify to the Public Accounts Committee but on which they have taken action which has not received publicity: surplus assets disposal- heading here is not in keeping with committee's recommendation which deals with the costing of material inventories; the Treasury Board has given approval in principle to the establishment of a working capital advance for the purpose of costing and controlling Department of National Defence material inventories; proposed removal allowance-the Treasury Board is conducting a study into the feasibility of applying this recommendation to the whole of the public service and not just to the armed forces; increasing accommodation rental costs-the Auditor General's report for 1971 states that the Department of Public Works circularized departments in 1971 advising them that it would use 1972-73 as a pilot year to refine techniques with the intention, subject to Treasury Board approval, to commence charging for accommodation on April 1, 1973.

Mr. Speaker, this proves that one way or another the government has followed up on the 38 recommendations that the Auditor General's report contained and which some hon. members have talked about today.

Since I was not a member of that committee while the hon. member was chairman, I am not in a position to make any remarks on its non partisan activity, but, if I consider his activity in this House, I cannot agree with him on the meaning of the term non partisan.

Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes remaining this afternoon I shall not attempt to deal with the litany recited over the last 10 or 15 minutes by my colleague on the other side: it was very selective, but the fact is that the Auditor General made it perfectly clear that of the 41 items set out in his report, 31 have not been dealt with-and the recitation by the hon. member will not erase them. In recent years this government has paid little attention to the report of the Auditor General.

May 26, 1972
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys
I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), and in part with the remarks of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland). The motion before us reads:
This House, noting the continuing erosion of Parliament's control over government spending of public moneys due to government evasion of constitutional and legal safeguards as noted in the 1970-71 report of the Auditor General, and due to imperfect procedural structure, reaffirms the fundamental principle of the Canadian constitution that Parliament must control expenditures of public moneys.
The remarks made this afternoon by hon. members opposite in an attempt to refute that motion have not been effective. I suggest that hon. members have no option but to support the motion. The Auditor General quite clearly pointed out many inefficiencies. I could recite the case of keeping open CFB Summerside in respect of which the Auditor General has clearly stated that money is being used for purposes not completely approved by Parliament.
The question of control by this House over the pursestrings of Canada is not an old issue, as was mentioned by my colleagues the hon. member for St. John's East and the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates). I have been here for only seven or eight years but have followed the procedures of this House with respect to control of government spending. It has been demonstrated, as these hon. members pointed out, that until this government started toying with our rules and procedures there was ample control over the expenditure of moneys by government; there was the power and procedure to deal with estimates. But that power has been taken away to the extent that now we have no way of influencing government spending. Even those of us who have been here only a short time are aware of this.
Questions such as the one put to the government by the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North, with respect to the St. Lawrence Seaway, impel me to rise this afternoon and express my concern. When the St. Lawrence Seaway was built in 1959-60 a very firm and clear undertaking was given to the ports of Atlantic Canada that it would pay its own way and would not be detrimental to the operations of the ports of Halifax, Saint John, and some of the lower St. Lawrence River ports.
We have not only the observation of the Auditor General in his most recent report for the year 1971 but we have other evidence to indicate that the government has failed utterly and miserably in this respect. It would appear that the St. Lawrence Seaway will be able to pay its way. The absence of control by this House over methods of correcting the situation is reflected in that failure. We have no control over government and there is no way that we can withhold money, for example, from the Minister of Transport. At the end of May the estimates will be passed whether we have seen them or not. Today it was suggested that two or three of them should come to the House. Whilst this is a good suggestion, it only goes part way.

Canadians in British Columbia, Newfoundland, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba-indeed everywhere-are picking up a debt of some $656 million. The tolls on the seaway do not even approach coverage of the interest. Who is paying for this? It is written off, according to the reply to a question of the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North regarding the situation at the end of this year. The official reply concluded with the statement:
In 1970, the United States government revised the financial structure of the American counterpart to Canada's seaway authority, the St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation, so as to require the corporation to only cover annual operation and maintenance costs and repay the original capital costs of construction-accrued and future interest obligations were waived. This approach, along with other proposals, such as those contained in the Carr report, present themselves as possibilities for altering the present system of repayment of the outstanding obligations of the seaway authority.
Without some appropriate control over the method in which the government spends the taxpayers' money, I suggest that the motion of the hon. member for Peace River is correct and necessary. As things stand, people in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, British Columbia and elsewhere are being asked to pick up that debt. The government is saying that our friends to the south have an excellent solution which they will take as their own and which they have used as an official response to questions on this subject.
Seven years ago in this House I suggested that the seaway toll should be written off over a 75 or 100-year period. That would cover the cost of handling the money which represents a great debt in terms of interest only, not in terms of capital that has gone out. I suggest that is not fair to the people of the Atlantic area since over the years the effect on the ports of Saint John, New Brunswick, Halifax, St. John's, Newfoundland, and Corner Brook will be detrimental.

May 26, 1972

Further, I support the motion before the House because the Auditor General has once again found it necessary to remind us of the way this government had dealt with his staff, auditors and senior administrators. As has been said this afternoon, members of this House are obligated to that officer. We are obligated to do everything within our power for him in order that he may continue fulfilling that function which has been effectively removed from us.
I know the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) would like to take away the responsibilities the Auditor General has to this chamber. The minister has curtailed the responsibilities of the opposition. He has not been able to do that to the Auditor General and I hope he will not be able to in the future. If the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), the only minister in the chamber, is to speak later I hope he will comment on the paragraph in the Auditor General's report relating directly, I suggest, to the motion before us. Specifically, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that there are 35 references in Mr. Henderson's report dealing with the Department of National Defence and these references relate directly to the motion.
During the last three or four years the department has had no alternative but to plan its own demise as a result of a frozen defence budget. I suggest that a minister owes it to the armed forces and members of this House to say how the government intends to unfreeze the defence budget so that those errors, omissions and infractions about which the Auditor General spoke can be overcome within the Department of National Defence. Many of that department's troubles have resulted from inadequate funds.
The government should make clear the procedures it intends to use to restore to this chamber its previous rights. Hon. members ought to be able to discuss government spending fully and their views ought to be given teeth. Only then will we get back on track, and only then can members advise, scrutinize and give consideration to the spending of taxpayers' dollars before they are wasted. I submit the motion is supportable. Anyone who has been in this chamber for more than two or three years cannot take any position other than that suggested in the motion.
The power and authority of this House over spending has been eroded. Those are not our words, they are words which have been analysed and spelled out clearly by the Auditor General. I think we all owe to that officer the support which this motion implicitly gives him, no matter whether it comes to a vote or not. I suggest that government supporters, if they have retained any influence in caucus, ought to persuade their ministers to support the Auditor General. They, too, are under that obligation, an obligation which is implicit in the words of the motion moved by the hon. member for Peace River. If we fail to support that officer, programs like the St. Lawrence Seaway may be thrust upon us without adequate examination or opportunity for meaningful scrutiny by this chamber.
At present, although we can ask questions and make our views known we are not given power. We on this side ought to be able to hold up the expenditures of one or more departments. At least it should be two or three and
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys
preferably that power ought to extend to all departments of government. After ail, that is why we are here. We are not here to do the government's work; we are here to check on the work of government.
In recent years this chamber has become nothing but a housekeeping institution. The committees are housekeeping institutions. If a committee wishes to impress its point of view on the government, there is no way of doing it. The same can be said of this chamber. For these reasons, if the matter came to a vote I would wholeheartedly support the motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise before this large audience, not to make a very important speech from the philosophical or constitutional point of view nor to deal with the rights and duties of Parliament and of the Auditor General.
From the philosophical point of view, I have only one remark to make: it is human to err and the government of Canada has certainly made mistakes, as have the governments of all other countries, which does not mean that all governments are bad but only that some are worse than others.
Therefore, I do not rise to deal with very elevated subjects. I simply want to make a very modest contribution to political science students in the country who, reading the report of this afternoon's proceedings, especially the remarks made by hon. members of the opposition, might think that everything the Auditor General has revealed is catastrophic in nature and conclude that Canada has the worst government ever since the remote times of Roman history.
-Then I shall simply deal with cases regarding my department and this, again, as a contribution to political science in Canada. I shall quickly go over the Auditor General's criticisms against my department. I had this study made only today. It is pretty sketchy but I want to give it to the House anyway. At page 87-

In paragraph 87 there is the heading, "Failure to collect revenue due to the Crown because of inadequate control over contracts." Mr. Speaker, under this heading the Auditor General observes that many of the DIP contracts-Defence Industry Productivity- contained repayment provisions and that the department had not followed up to collect moneys due. His current comment deplores the lack of action on the part of the department in following up. The reasons for delay in following up were explained to the Public Accounts Committee last November. Action was initiated last September and progress was reported to the chairman of that committee by the minister, by myself, last May.
Here is a situation which has repeated itself on a number of occasions. The accusation has been made. The minister has confessed and atoned, but the accusation is repeated. No absolution is given, notwithstanding contrition. The sinner is reminded of his sin year after year even if he has confessed, made amends and paid in lost pride. That is the first case deplored by the Auditor General.

May 26, 1972
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys
I said I was making a contribution to students of political science in Canada. The second case, paragraph 88, concerns grants to the Standards Council of Canada. The Auditor General here considers that the unspent portion of the grant to the Standards Council should have lapsed at the end of the fiscal year. He very sweetly says that this is an "opinion". It just so happens that we in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce obtained legal advice and got a different opinion. This being a grant, the opinion given to us was that the money belonged to the Standards Council of Canada. It not being an agent of Her Majesty it is not subject to the lapsing provisions of section 30 of the Financial Administration Act. The Auditor General has some lawyers on his side, we have some on our side, and that is all there is to it.
Paragraph 89, "Taxation of recaptured capital cost allowance with respect to vessels sold": this is a complicated matter. One aspect has to do with the administration of shipbuilding provisions in the Income Tax Act and in my own departmental subsidy program. It so happened that one agency of the Crown purchased a ship. It asked for the subsidy and we gave it under the provision of the law, notwithstanding the fact that it was a corporation of the Crown. The purpose of the law is to create employment in Canada. That corporation is free to go wherever it pleases to buy a ship. If we want to prevent a corporation of the Crown from buying a ship elsewhere than in Canada, we have to provide the normal subsidy to the agency of the Crown as we would to a private individual. That covers the third item.
The fourth item has to do with concessions made to motor vehicle manufacturers. The Auditor General observed that one major manufacturer did not meet the conditions of a conditional remission order. The manufacturer became liable for duty and sales tax amounting to $6 million. This amount is not included in the accounts receivable of the Department of National Revenue and that department states that it expects the debt to be forgiven. The failure was of a technical nature related to the Canadian value added in vehicles manufactured in Canada. The manufacturer concerned more than compensated for this deficiency by the export of automotive parts and hence met the over-all objectives of the automotive program. An order in council regularizing the situation has been promulgated.
In this case one has a choice between using the letter of the law and the spirit of the law. It is not always easy to decide. Had we made a strict interpretation of the law and the regulations, we probably would have been accused by the opposition of presiding over the failure of that company, depriving people of their employment. We decided to be intelligent about this, use our heads and we now stand to be chastised by the Auditor General for having done so. I suggest that the opposition would have done as we did. When you read the Auditor General's report it sounds nasty, awful, crooked and immoral, but I am telling hon. members the truth and leave it to them to judge.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
No, not at all. I feel I am making a little contribution to political science and public opinion in

Canada. I have not done so for at least a few days; this afternoon before five o'clock is not a bad time or a bad place to do so. If I am showing excessive modesty, it must be because of the limited number of members sitting opposite.
Paragraph 152 is another case, a rather complicated one. I answered this question this morning. The Auditor General observes here that in the case of the machinery program there has been a departure from normal practice in that the names of companies receiving remissions have not been shown in the public accounts.
The practice followed in 1971 is the same as that followed in previous years. The order in council numbers are shown in the public accounts report. There are approximately 17,000 remissions per annum. To publish them in the public accounts would be impractical. Company names and amounts can be obtained from the order in council concerned, which are in the public domain. We believe the practice to be consistent with the requirements of the Financial Administration Act.
This is a straight formality. Presumably the Auditor General would have liked us to publish the 17,000 names in the public accounts. We think this would unnecessarily crowd the public accounts. We publish in the accounts the number of PC orders, and these are available. I presume that someone reading these accusations might think that there is something devilish, "nasty, brutish and short" about what we have done here. Such is not the case.
I wish to draw another example to Your Honour's attention. I know that Your Honour is also a student of political science. Paragraph 166 has to do with the cost of unused space in Montreal, Quebec and Toronto, Ontario. The Auditor General observes that the closure of design centres in Montreal and Toronto cost the Crown $150,700 and $9,100 respectively in non-productive costs. This is under the design program of my department.
The design centres were open in Montreal and Toronto for a number of years. At first they were relatively well attended. However, public interest decreased and when we cost-benefited the whole thing it was found that every person visiting the design centre cost the government $5. It was decided that this was not very practical and the design program of my department was reoriented. It is now aimed at developing design in the manufacturing sector as opposed to educating the public sector as to its importance.
When the decision was made it was well known that the closure of the design centres would cost $150,000. The decision was made bearing this in mind. There was nothing "nasty, brutish and short" about that particular decision.
Paragraph 260 concerns advances, loans and investments, domestic, miscellaneous, loans to manufacturers re defence plant modernization. The situation here is that defence manufacturers are eligible for loans to purchase machinery for plant modernization. When a manufacturer defaults on repayment, the machinery is repossessed and the loan is extinguished. The Auditor General observes that equipment was repossessed and yet is still shown as a receivable in the public accounts.
May 26, 1972

The reply is again simple. In all but one case the department has been able to sell the repossessed machinery for the amount owing: in all cases except one we have been able to repossess and sell. It is quite normal, then, to treat a repossessed machine as something which is saleable. We consider it to be an asset. It would be misleading to the public to write the equipment concerned down to zero when there is every expectation of recovery. There is no provision in the government's accounting system to show an asset at market value. The least misleading approach is to show it as a receivable. Equipment not sold after one year is written off.
That is my contribution. I have just dealt with most of the items in the Auditor General's report that pertain to my department. I agree that it has been a skimpy explanation. I am just trying to demonstrate that when reading these accounts one should not hit the roof each time he sees an item. I am not generalizing; I am being very objective. I am just saying that these condemnations or observations should be placed in the proper context. I have tried to demonstrate that this afternoon so that students of political science now and in the future will not think that this government has no respect for efficiency and responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, this debate is drawing to a close, and I think it has been a very good one. I want to pay tribute to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) who has just resumed his seat. I think he did what the Auditor
Alleged Loss of Control of Public Moneys
General has been trying to do for years; he got to his feet and explained the items that affected him. He told us of his problems and his difficulties and in some cases he asked forgiveness. As one member of the opposition, I felt he was most constructive and I congratulate him. He dealt with about six items. And six from 41 leaves 35; therefore I hope he will prevail upon his colleagues to do what he has done. If so, then the Auditor General has done his job and we in Parliament have done our job.
I think the government has approached this matter in the wrong way and has done so from the beginning. The present Auditor General has criticized former governments, not out of a sense of partisanship but because it is his duty under the law to bring these criticisms forward.
In closing, I think we have had a good afternoon and that the minister deserves credit for what he did. I only hope that his colleagues in the cabinet; some of whom are affected more seriously than others, will do what the minister did. I also hope that more than political scientists will follow this debate and pay attention to the confessions the minister has just made.
